title: The click
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino asks what makes a concept click for students after a teacher has planned, modelled and checked well. She starts from her own memory of failing to understand chemical bonding at school despite working hard and answering routine questions. She then sets out a three-step response. First, checks for understanding should probe linked reasoning, not just recall, using a worked example from arteries and veins. Second, retrieval practice must permeate lessons and connect ideas, rather than being a one-off starter on isolated facts. Third, rehearsal, where students explain concepts verbally or in writing, deepens understanding, provided earlier steps have secured the knowledge. The piece is a candid classroom-practice reflection grounded in schema theory.
points: Recall questions can mask a lack of understanding, so checks for understanding should require students to link facts, explain structure and function, and predict consequences.
Retrieval practice works when it is woven through lessons and joins ideas into schemas, not when done occasionally on isolated facts.
Rehearsal through explanation and discussion extends understanding but only after knowledge is secure, or it cements misconceptions.
Castelino's own failure to grasp bonding despite diligence shows that apparent success in class can be an illusion of knowing.
quotes: What was my barrier back then? I worked hard. I practised loads. I did my homework. My classmates apparently got it so the teacher’s instructions could not be the issue.

These questions are only checking recall, which is important too. I do want my students to remember key facts so I can build on this knowledge. However, I can take this further and situate the new learning into context, linking key facts together.

No, retrieval practice needs to permeate our teaching. It needs to be consistently practiced and students need to connect knowledge together all the time. There may be the odd fact that cannot be tethered to something learnt previously but most of what we teach needs to form connections in our students’ memories. We are training students to build schemas and retrieve bigger chunks of knowledge, not just isolated facts.
If like past-me, you ‘do retrieval’ once or twice and mostly of isolated facts, it won’t work. Students will probably not experience true understanding of knowledge.

Before students can rehearse what they are have learnt and understood, it is important that the previous steps of CFUs and retrieval practice are followed well. If knowledge isn’t completely secure, there is a danger that students could be rehearsing the wrong things, cementing misconceptions or errors into their schemas.

I feel more confident that students get something when I have explained a concept clearly, checked for understanding, encouraged deep retrieval practice and got students to rehearse their understanding. Hopefully, in the process, students feel it all clicks.
